lead: A crew works by shared words. When the skipper calls "ease the genoa" or "fender on the port quarter", everyone must picture the same thing. These are the names you need on board, grouped the way you meet them.

blocks.p: **Port** is the left side of the boat when you face forward, **starboard** the right, whichever way you are looking. The **bow** is the front, the **stern** the back. Something at right angles to the boat is **abeam**; between the beam and the stern it is on the **quarter**. A boat close to your heading line is fine on the bow.

fig.note: Named from the boat, facing forward

blocks.p: **Windward** is the side the wind comes from, **leeward** the side it blows to: sit to windward, be sick to leeward. A **lee shore** has the wind blowing onto it, so keep well off. **Fore-and-aft** means along the boat, **athwartships** across it.

The **pulpit** is the rail round the bow, the **pushpit** the rail round the stern, and **stanchions** carry the guardwires between them. You go below through the **companionway**, closed with washboards in a big sea.

head: Measure
Why it matters
rows: Keel depth below the waterline: compare it with the depth at low water
Masthead height above the water: bridges
The widest point: berths; a catamaran is twice as wide
Hull above the water: more of it, more windage
Weight: a heavy boat carries her way longer

blocks.p: A **fin keel** turns tightly, a **long keel** holds a straight course, **twin keels** let a boat sit upright on the mud. A catamaran has no ballast keel: she barely heels, so you reef by the wind speed, and she does not right herself after a capsize.

**Standing rigging** holds the mast: the **forestay** forward, the **backstay** aft, the **shrouds** to each side, spread by the **spreaders** and fixed to **chainplates** in the deck through **bottlescrews**. The **gooseneck** is the hinge between boom and mast. If a windward shroud breaks, tack at once to put the load on the sound side; if the forestay goes, bear away onto a run.

head: Line
What it does
rows: Trims it in and out; on a genoa it goes to the clew
Flattens the foot of the main
Holds the boom down off the wind
Holds the boom up when the sail is down
Lets the boom down to leeward in a gust

blocks.p: To **reef**: ease the mainsheet and kicker, lower the halyard, hook on the new tack, haul the reefing line to bring the new clew to the boom, hoist tight again. Take a loaded line on a winch before you open its clutch.

No boat sails straight into the wind: about 45° either side of it is the **no-go zone**. From its edge round to dead downwind every course has a name. Between close-hauled and a beam reach lies the **close reach**.
The **tack** is named after the side the wind comes over: all four boats above are on port tack. On a run it is the side opposite the boom.

**Luffing up** turns the bow towards the wind, **bearing away** turns it from the wind. A **tack** takes the bow through the wind: call "lee-ho" and release the old genoa sheet as the bow comes through. A **gybe** takes the stern through: centre the mainsheet first, so the boom cannot slam across. In strong wind, tack round instead.

fig.note: In irons: head to wind, stopped

blocks.p: Stopped head to wind you are **in irons**: back the jib to push the bow off. To **heave to**, tack without releasing the genoa and lash the helm to turn up: the boat lies quietly but drifts to leeward. A **preventer** holds the boom forward on a run.

sections.title: Ease until it luffs, then trim in

blocks.p: A sail works best on the edge of luffing: ease it until the front edge just flutters, then trim in a little. Sheeted too hard it stalls, heels the boat and slows her. Light wind wants fuller sails; strong wind flatter ones with more twist.

head: What you see
What you do
rows: The sail is stalled: ease the sheet
Top of the genoa luffs first
Let the traveller down, then reef

blocks.rule: Reef early, in sheltered water, before the wind arrives. If you are wondering whether to reef, it is time.
blocks.label: Remember
